title: Picked for height, sorted by birthday
hook: Every child in the league is nine. Does the month they were born in matter?

knows: older children in a class are a bit bigger
doesNotKnow: that picking the 'best' from a one-year age band, with a fixed cutoff date, selects for birth month: the children born just after the cutoff are up to a year older than their rivals

misconception: A birth month can't matter much when every child in the band is 'the same age'.
objective: The learner can explain that when a league picks the tallest 10% of a one-year band with a 1 January cutoff, about 44% of the picks (in the lesson's model) are born January to March instead of 25%, that the peak follows the cutoff when it moves, and that a less selective pick (top 50%) shows a smaller skew.

claims.text: Outliers argues that selection under the 1 January age cutoff is how Canadian hockey's elite came to skew toward early-year birthdays.
claims.source: Malcolm Gladwell, Outliers: The Story of Success (Little, Brown, 2008), work gladwell-outliers-2008, ch. 1 'The Matthew Effect' (unconfirmed). The book argues this; the claim is about the book, not the world. Our own words; no quote. The book also argues that extra coaching after selection widens the gap; that half is not shown on the stage and not stated in the reveal. Brief: company/domains/briefs/books.md #3.

claims.text: The book's hockey example draws on research on birthdates of Canadian hockey players (the relative age effect).
claims.source: Barnsley, Thompson & Barnsley (1985), 'Hockey success and birthdate: the relative age effect', CAHPER Journal 51(8) (to confirm). Not stated to the learner beyond the book claim; recorded because the book uses it (charter: cite the study for the result).

claims.text: Does it hold up? Yes: the relative age effect, an over-representation of relatively older players in age-grouped sport, is one of sport science's best-replicated findings.
claims.source: Cobley, Baker, Wattie & McKenna (2009), 'Annual age-grouping and athlete development: a meta-analytical review of relative age effects in sport', Sports Medicine 39(3). Verdict 'holds up' is the brief drafter's reading, for the fact-checker.

claims.text: The heights are the lesson's model (stage chip 'Model: +0.5 cm per month older, ±5.5 cm spread'): births spread evenly over the year, height rises 0.5 cm per month of age within the band, with a normal spread of 5.5 cm.
claims.source: Lesson model, Demo.tsx picksByK(); the numbers are the brief's illustrative choice, not measured growth data.

claims.text: In the model, picking the top 10% with a 1 January cutoff gives 44% of the picks born January to March (a fair split would give 25%) and 10% born October to December; picking the top 50% gives 33% January to March; moving the cutoff moves the peak to the months just after it.
claims.source: Analytic model, Demo.tsx (threshold by bisection, normal tail): top 10%: Jan–Mar 43.9%, Oct–Dec 10.1%; top 50%: Jan–Mar 32.9%. Builder node run 2026-10-14 (scratch rae.mjs); brief check company/domains/briefs/checks/books-cycle1-check.mjs gives 43.9 / 10.1. The cutoff shift is a relabelling of months, so the peak follows the cutoff exactly.

claims.text: With a 1 September cutoff and selection of the strongest, children born in September to November are over-represented, because they are the oldest in their band.
claims.source: Same model as c5 with the cutoff relabelled; c3 for the real-world effect.

recall.question: A school's football team picks its strongest players from each school year. The year runs from 1 September. Which birth months will be most common on the team?
recall.why: Children born just after the 1 September cutoff are the oldest in their year, so picking the strongest over-selects them.
